title: One Drop, Right Eye, Three Times a Day

patient.name: Mr Lim Chin Huat
patient.presenting_complaint: Newly diagnosed with glaucoma in the right eye and prescribed eye drops for the first time — needs to learn how to use them correctly

history.hpc: Mr Lim was seen by the doctor today and diagnosed with primary open-angle glaucoma in the right eye. He has been prescribed latanoprost 0.005% eye drops, one drop to the right eye every night. He has never used eye drops before and is nervous about putting anything in his eye. He mentions he sometimes has trouble with his hands shaking slightly. He asks the OA to show him how to do it before he goes home.
history.pmhx: Newly diagnosed primary open-angle glaucoma, right eye. Hypertension. Mild essential tremor in both hands (longstanding, not on treatment).
history.allergies: No drug allergy recorded on file.
history.family_hx: Father had glaucoma and used eye drops for many years
medications: New: Latanoprost 0.005% eye drops, one drop right eye at night
history.social_hx: Lives alone. Independent with daily activities but has mild hand tremor.

examination_findings.anterior_segment: Normal bilaterally. No allergic conjunctivitis or signs of drop intolerance (first dose not yet given).
examination_findings.fundus: Glaucomatous optic disc changes noted in right eye by doctor — cup-to-disc ratio increased compared to left

investigations.iop_nct: RE: 26 mmHg (elevated). LE: 19 mmHg (upper normal). Confirms need for IOP-lowering treatment in the right eye.
investigations.drop_technique_assessment: Patient demonstrates instillation technique under OA supervision: initial attempt shows patient tilting head back insufficiently and aiming drop directly at the cornea, causing him to blink and miss. With coaching on pulling down the lower lid to create a pocket and aiming for the lower fornix, second attempt is successful with one drop correctly instilled into the lower conjunctival sac.

diagnosis: New diagnosis of primary open-angle glaucoma, right eye, IOP 26 mmHg, requiring topical latanoprost. Patient is a first-time eye drop user with mild hand tremor — correct instillation technique must be taught and confirmed before discharge.

immediate: Confirm the diagnosis, the eye to be treated (right eye only), the drop name, strength, and frequency (latanoprost 0.005%, one drop right eye at night)
Check the patient is not allergic to the medication or its preservatives

Explain the procedure step by step before demonstrating: wash hands, tilt head back or lie down, look up, gently pull down the lower eyelid to form a pocket, instil one drop into the lower fornix without touching the bottle tip to the eye or lashes
Demonstrate the technique using a practice/demo bottle if available, then observe the patient performing it themselves
Coach the patient through correction of his initial technique error (aiming at cornea instead of lower fornix)
Advise him to apply gentle pressure over the inner corner of the eye (nasolacrimal duct) for about 1 minute after instillation to reduce systemic absorption
Confirm the patient can correctly identify the right eye and demonstrate the technique successfully before he leaves
Document that drop teaching was given, technique demonstrated, and patient successfully return-demonstrated correct technique
follow_up: Doctor to review IOP response to latanoprost at next follow-up visit
If hand tremor makes instillation consistently difficult, consider involving a family member or exploring drop-aid devices at a future visit
Schedule follow-up appointment for IOP recheck
patient_education: Use latanoprost one drop in the right eye every night at the same time, even if the eye feels normal — glaucoma has no symptoms
Do not stop the drops without speaking to the doctor, even if vision seems fine
Store the drops as per the label instructions and note how long the bottle has been open
Common side effects include mild stinging, redness, and gradual darkening/lengthening of eyelashes — these are usually not concerning, but he should mention them at follow-up
If he has difficulty due to his hand tremor, he can ask a family member to help or discuss drop-aid devices with the team

key_points: Confirms the new diagnosis, the correct eye, and the prescribed medication name/strength/frequency
Checks for known drug allergies before instillation
Identifies the patient's hand tremor as a factor that may affect his ability to self-administer drops
Establishes that this is the patient's first time using eye drops
Reviews the documented IOP findings (26 mmHg right eye) that justify the new treatment
Assesses the patient's actual instillation technique through observation/return-demonstration, not just verbal explanation
Identifies the specific technique error (aiming at the cornea instead of the lower fornix)
Documents the outcome of the technique assessment
Recognises this is a teaching/competency case, not a diagnostic dilemma — diagnosis (POAG, right eye) is already established
Identifies that correct technique is essential for the treatment to be effective
Recognises the hand tremor as a potential ongoing barrier to correct self-administration
Understands that confirming successful return-demonstration is part of safe discharge
Follows the correct instillation procedure: confirm diagnosis/purpose/eye, check allergy, explain, demonstrate, supervise return-demonstration
Coaches the patient to correct his technique (lower fornix, not cornea) and confirms successful instillation
Teaches punctal occlusion (pressure on inner corner) to reduce systemic absorption
Provides clear medication adherence education appropriate for an asymptomatic chronic condition (glaucoma)
Documents teaching given and competency demonstrated
